chapters.title: What never goes into an AI tool

obj.label: Text assistant · New chat
obj.subject: Draft a reply to a complaint
lines: Phone number for the call back

say.text: Monday, five past eight. A complaint from a customer is waiting in the office. The reply should be friendly but firm, so the whole email goes into the text assistant. It takes ten seconds.

data.text: Is someone in your office about to paste a *customer complaint* into an AI tool?
data.sub: Five kinds of data that never go in, and one rule for everything else.

say.text: Is someone in your office about to paste a customer complaint into an AI tool?
Five kinds of data that never go in, and one rule for everything else.

items.title: The list and the rule of doubt
What do you do? Two cases

say.text: We go like this: an ordinary day, the list and the rule of doubt, the sources, two cases in which you decide, the example business, what all of this is not, and at the end two free tools.

data.text: Nobody decided any of this. It happened, *one task at a time*.
data.sub: Three in the office use a text assistant, two field staff privately on their phones.

say.text: We use one fictional business in every video: an electrical contractor with ten to forty-nine staff in Austria. Nobody in it is real. Three people in the office use a text assistant for quotes, summaries and translations. Two field staff set the same assistant up privately on their phones. Nobody decided any of this. It happened, one task at a time.

data.headline: What goes in on an *ordinary day*
data.note: Each person decided alone, in the moment.

doc.label: Inputs · one day · example
doc.title: None of this was meant badly

lines.text: Complaint letter with name, address, site
Calculation sheet for a job
Access code to a customer's building
A colleague's sick note

say.text: Now look at what goes in on an ordinary day. A complaint letter to a customer, with the name, the address and what went wrong on site. A calculation sheet for a job, because the assistant is good at tidying up tables. The access code to a customer's building, because it sat in the same email as the job description. A colleague's sick note, to shorten it for the file. None of this was meant badly. Each person decided alone, in the moment, with nothing to lean on.

items.title: Personal data
items.sub: entering and transferring each need a legal basis

items.title: Trade secrets
items.sub: only with reasonable steps to keep them secret

items.title: An access code in a tool
items.sub: is an access code out of your hands

say.text: Three things follow.

First: details that identify a customer, an employee or an applicant are personal data. Entering them into an AI application, and transferring them to the provider, each need a legal basis under the GDPR.
Second: calculations, prices, contracts and customer lists are trade secrets only while the business takes reasonable steps to keep them secret.
Third: an access code in a tool is an access code out of your hands.

data.text: A rule moves the decision from the keyboard to the *business*.
data.sub: Once, in writing: the list, the rule of doubt, two tools.

say.text: Our interpretation: a rule moves that decision from each person at the keyboard to the business, once, in writing. That is what this video is about: the list, the rule of doubt, and two tools you can hand to your staff tomorrow.

chapters.title: The list and the rule of doubt

data.headline: Five kinds of data *never* go into an AI tool

items.title: Customers, staff, applicants
items.sub: names, addresses, dates of birth, customer numbers, licence plates

items.title: Health data
items.sub: sick note, diagnosis, a word like “surgery”

say.text: Here is the list: section three of the usage policy in the AI Policy Toolkit, the same for every business. Five kinds of data never go into an AI tool, whatever the access.
One. Details about customers, staff and applicants by which a person can be identified: names, addresses, dates of birth, customer numbers, a licence plate.
Two. Access data: passwords, keys, access codes, tokens.
Three. Calculations, prices, contracts, customer lists and everything else the business keeps confidential.
Four. Health data: a sick note, a diagnosis, a word like "surgery" in an email about a colleague.
Five. Documents of third parties handed over in confidence: a customer's plans, a tender with a confidentiality clause.

rows.text: the app on a private phone
private accounts and devices: individual profiles
add your own kinds in your own words

say.text: "Whatever the access" is the important part: the business account, a private account, the app on a private phone. The German data protection authorities advise that employees should not have to work through private accounts and devices, because profiles of individual employees can arise that way.
The business adds its own kinds, in its own words, so that the people who handle them recognise them.

data.kicker: The rule that closes the list
data.text: In doubt, enter nothing, and ask the *named person*.
data.sub: That person must be reachable. That is why the rule stands first on the one page.

say.text: Then comes the rule that closes the list. In doubt, enter nothing, and ask the named person. Our interpretation: a list without a rule of doubt is incomplete, because no catalogue meets every case. The rule only works if that person is reachable, in person or by phone. That is why it stands first on the one page, above the list.

data.headline: When the *personal data* cannot be split off

items.title: Not with an AI tool at all
Only in an approved tool
items.sub: the register approves it for personal data

say.text: Some tasks involve a person and cannot be split from it. The policy gives the business three ways to choose from. A task with personal data is not done with an AI tool at all. Or the text is drafted with placeholders and the details are inserted afterwards, outside the tool. Or the task is done only in a tool that the register approves for personal data.

data.text: Removing names and addresses is regularly not enough; the *connection to a person* can be restored from the context.
data.origin: Paraphrased from: Datenschutzkonferenz, guidance on AI and data protection, 6 May 2024, section 3.1, p. 12

say.text: Why not just delete the name? Because that is regularly not enough. The data protection authorities state that removing names and addresses from an input often leaves the person identifiable, since the connection can be restored from the context, especially with applications whose purpose is to create cross-references from unstructured data.

data.headline: The *placeholder rule*
data.note: Date, street and job can also point to a person.

lines.text: about our visit on [date] at [site]
we regret that …
Somebody inserts the details afterwards, outside the tool

say.text: The placeholder rule is the practical middle way for a small business. You write the complaint with "customer" and "site" in square brackets instead of the details. Afterwards, outside the tool, somebody inserts them. The date of the visit, the street and the job can still point to a person, so the placeholders cover those too, not only the name.

data.kicker: One more habit belongs to it
data.sub: Figures, names, deadlines and references are read by the person who uses the result.

say.text: One more habit belongs to the list: check before use. Figures, names, deadlines and references are read and checked by the person who uses the result, every time. The BSI, the German Federal Office for Information Security, asks that users can question the outputs of a model critically, adjust them where needed and restrict their reuse.

data.headline: Free tool 1: *“May this go in?”*
data.note: Runs in your browser and sends nothing.

lines.text: What is in the text or file?
Which account would you use?
Does the provider train on your inputs?
What is the task?
Red: no · Amber: clarify first · Green: yes, with a check

say.text: Two free tools turn this into something your staff can use today. Both run in your browser and send nothing anywhere. The first is called "May this go in?". Four questions: what is in the text or file, which account you would use, whether the provider trains its models on your inputs, and what the task is. You tick, and a traffic light answers. Red: no, not like this. Amber: not yet, clarify first. Green: yes, with the usual check. Under the light stand the reasons and what to do instead.

data.text: No AI for *decisions about a person*.
data.sub: Hiring, assessment, promotion, termination, task allocation: high-risk under Annex III.

say.text: The fourth question catches a case the list does not: a decision about a person. Hiring, assessment, promotion, termination, task allocation. AI tools are not used for that, whatever the data. Annex three of the AI Act lists systems for recruitment, selection, promotion, termination, task allocation and monitoring as high-risk.

data.headline: Free tool 2: *“Is there anything personal in it?”*

lines.text: Email addresses, phone numbers, IBANs
Names, addresses, health terms, access data
One click replaces them with placeholders
Limit: finds patterns, not everything

say.text: The second tool is called "Is there anything personal in it?". You paste a text. While you type, it marks email addresses, phone numbers, IBANs, names, addresses, health terms and access data. One click replaces them with placeholders. Its limit is stated on the page: it finds patterns. A name without a salutation, a nickname, a rare job title or an address without a house number can stay unmarked. Treat green as nothing obvious.

data.headline: The list rests on *two German bodies*

say.text: Now the sources, with their markers.

The list rests on two German bodies. The data protection authorities recommend clear, documented internal rules on whether, under which conditions and for which purposes which AI applications may be used.
The BSI asks employers to lay down which inputs are permitted and how outputs may be reused, bindingly, for example in policies.
Our interpretation: both bodies are German. Their recommendations are professional practice, not law, and bind nobody outside Germany.

lines.text: a  secret, not generally known
b  commercial value because it is secret
c  reasonable steps to keep it secret
Austria: UWG · Germany: GeschGehG

say.text: The strongest reason for the list is the trade secret. Under the Trade Secrets Directive, information is a trade secret only if it meets three conditions. The third: it has been subject to reasonable steps, under the circumstances, to keep it secret. Austria implements this in its Unfair Competition Act, Germany in its Trade Secrets Act.

data.text: Does a usage policy count as a *reasonable step*?
data.sub: Without a rule no evidence, with a rule a record. Whether reasonable: case by case.

say.text: This is open: whether a usage policy counts as such a reasonable step. We searched no court decision on this question. The handbook therefore says only this: without a rule, there is no evidence that the business took any step at all; with a rule, the business can show that it did. Whether that step is reasonable is decided case by case.

data.text: Health data are a *special category*: processing is prohibited unless an exception in paragraph 2 applies.

say.text: Health data have their own rule. Article nine of the GDPR makes them a special category: processing is prohibited unless one of the exceptions in paragraph two applies.

items.text: into a tool that is not approved
notify the authority, unless no risk

say.text: And if it happens anyway: personal data that reach a tool or account the business has not approved can be a personal data breach. The controller notifies the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than seventy-two hours after becoming aware of it, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. Every breach is documented.

data.text: The report itself has *no consequences* for the person reporting.
data.sub: A business that punishes the report learns about incidents last.

say.text: Whether a given input is such a breach is decided case by case. That is why the policy says the report itself has no consequences for the person reporting: a business that punishes the report learns about incidents last.

chapters.title: What do you do? Two cases

data.place: Office, work instruction for the site team

obj.label: Email · Job
obj.subject: Wallbox in the underground car park, job
lines: Parking spaces 12 to 18, new supply line

say.text: Two cases for you to decide. Both are invented, the sources behind them are not. Case one. Tuesday, twenty past eleven. A job email is to be rewritten into a short work instruction for the field staff. The email also contains the code for the customer's underground car park.

options.text: Paste it, the code is not a password
Paste it, then delete the chat
Remove the code first, pass it on separately

say.text: What do you do? A: paste it, the code is not a password after all. B: paste it and delete the chat afterwards. C: remove the code first, replace it with a placeholder, and give it to the field staff another way. Think about it for a moment.

data.headline: Deleted from the chat, still out of the business

items.text: What the provider stores: in its terms
The code has left the business

say.text: B feels safe. In the example, the email is pasted at twenty-one minutes past eleven, code included, and three minutes later the chat is deleted.

What the provider does with the input and how long it keeps it is in its terms, not in the chat history. The only certain thing: the code has left the business. An access code in a tool is an access code out of your hands.

card.title: Code out, placeholder in
card.sub: Access data are on the list. The code goes to the field staff separately.

strikes.note: too late, the input is out

say.text: C is right. Access data are on the list, and access codes explicitly belong to them. A overlooks that, and B deletes too late, the input is already out. The work instruction can be written just as well with a placeholder; the field staff get the code through the channel the business uses for that.

obj.label: Message · Field technician
obj.subject: Off sick for two more weeks
lines: Two more weeks after the knee op
Please re-plan the School Lane site

say.text: Case two. Wednesday, ten to eight. A field technician writes that he is off sick for two more weeks after knee surgery, and asks for his site to be re-planned. The office manager wants a short note for the file and a new weekly plan from it.

options.text: Paste the message, leave out only the name
Delete the word “surgery”, paste the rest
No health data: [technician] not available from [date]

say.text: What do you do? A: paste the message and leave out only the name. B: delete the word surgery and paste the rest. C: paste nothing from the message and phrase the re-planning like this: one field technician not available for two weeks from a given date. Think about it for a moment.

data.headline: Without a name, but not without a person

items.text: Knee surgery, site, two weeks stay in
Everyone in the business knows who it is

say.text: A looks careful. In the example, only the name is missing. Knee surgery, site and two weeks are still in it, and in the business everyone knows at once who is meant.
So it remains health data about an identifiable person, and for that Article nine of the GDPR applies: processing is prohibited unless an exception applies.

card.title: Plan without health data
card.sub: The weekly plan needs who is missing, from when, how long. The reason stays out.

strikes.note: the context gives the person away
a sick note stays a sick note

say.text: C is right. For a weekly plan it is enough to know who is missing, from when and for how long; the reason does not belong in it. A fails because of the context, as with every input from which the person can be recognised. And B does not turn a sick note into a different message: a sick note stays health data. In case of doubt the rule from earlier applies: enter nothing, ask.

doc.label: Generator · example business
doc.title: Own kinds of data and ways

lines.text: Added: calculation sheets per job
Added: access codes to customer sites
Chosen: the placeholder rule
The office manager inserts the details afterwards

say.text: Back to the fictional business, called Example Electrical Ltd in the sample documents. In the generator it answered question D1 and added two kinds of its own: the calculation sheets per job, and the access codes to customer sites. For unavoidable personal data it chose the placeholder rule: the complaint is written with "customer" and "site" in brackets, and the office manager inserts the details afterwards.

data.headline: The hardest field: the *two field staff*

rows.text: work use on the private phone ends on the effective date

say.text: The two field staff with the private app were the hardest field. Our interpretation: a rule that only names the tool silently permits its use through a private account. So the rule names tool and access path, and the business had to choose: either the two get access through a business account, or their work use on the private phone ends on the effective date.

lines.text: Never into an AI tool: 5 + 2 kinds, each with a box
Only through the business access
Check before use, every time
It happened: report it, without consequences

say.text: This is what comes out of it for the wall: the one page. At the top, the rule of doubt: "In doubt: enter nothing, ask." Then "This never goes into an AI tool, whatever the access": the five kinds and the two the business added, each with a box to tick during the briefing. Then "Only through the business access." Then "Check before use, every time." Then "It happened: report it", with the sentence that the report itself has no consequences.
The page contains no section of the policy in full. Its content is taken from the policy and never decided separately, so that poster and policy cannot contradict each other.

data.sub: The traffic light decides nothing for your business. The check finds patterns.

say.text: What this is not. The sentence we use for the toolkit: it is not legal advice, and no document claims that your business complies with a rule. The documents show what you decided, since when, for which tools, and who knows about it.

The same goes for the two tools. The traffic light applies the nine areas of the usage policy; it is not legal advice and decides nothing on behalf of your business. The personal-data check finds patterns; treat green as nothing obvious.

rows.text: Policy as a reasonable step for secrecy?
other countries: chamber or data protection authority

say.text: What stays open. Whether a policy is a reasonable step to keep trade secrets: no court decision searched, open point eight twelve in the handbook.

And the toolkit checked Austria and Germany only. For other member states it names the gap and points you to your own chamber or data protection authority. Your business decides what goes on its list and who is asked.

chapters.title: Two free tools and the toolkit

rows.text: four questions, one light, before you paste
both in your browser, send nothing

say.text: Two things are free on scutoria.com, and the links are in the description. The tool "May this go in?": four questions, one traffic light, before you paste. The tool "Is there anything personal in it?": paste a text, see what identifies a person, replace it with placeholders. Both run in your browser and send nothing. Share the link with colleagues.

data.text: The rule *in writing*, with a date and a signature.
data.sub: Handbook online, readable before you buy · 199 euros per year · the first ten buyers pay 99

say.text: If you want the rule in writing, with a date and a signature: the AI Policy Toolkit. The usage policy with the list in section three and the placeholder rule in section four, the one page to post, the tool register, the briefing record and the evidence summary, generated from your answers. The handbook is online; read it before you buy. The toolkit costs 199 euros per year. The first ten buyers pay 99.

data.rule: This is Scutoria. Synthetic voice, sources on screen.

memo.label: Free: May this go in? · Anything personal in it?

say.text: This is Scutoria. The voice you hear is synthetic. The script was drafted with an AI tool, then checked by us, sentence by sentence. Every number and every legal statement carries its source on screen. Source-based, no legal advice.
